draft.title: Movements of people from 1750 to 1914
card: Between 1750 and 1914, millions of people moved from one part of the world to another. Some had a choice and some did not.
people moved against their will. Enslaved Africans were shipped to the Americas, and convicts were transported from Britain to colonies such as New South Wales.
people chose to move, hoping for a better life. They sought land to farm, gold, or paid work in new countries such as Australia and the United States.
The difference is choice. A person who is made to go is forced, even if they later build a life in the new place.
draft.remember: Millions moved in this period. Forced movement had no choice, free movement did.

a.q: Which person's journey was a forced movement?
opts: A convict sent from London to New South Wales
A farmer who sailed to Canada to buy cheap land
A miner who left Britain to look for gold in Victoria
A factory worker who moved abroad for better pay
a.why: The convict was sent by the government and had no choice. The farmer, the miner and the factory worker each chose to go, hoping for land, gold or work.
a.clue: Ask who made the decision to leave.

b.q: Tomas, a young man from Ireland, paid for his own ticket to Melbourne in the 1850s to find work. Why is his journey free movement, not forced?
opts: He chose to leave and was not made to go
He travelled by ship to a British colony
He was poor and had few choices at home
He later built a new life in Australia
b.why: Free movement means the person chose to go. Tomas decided to leave and paid his own way. Being poor or building a life in a new place does not decide it, since a forced person might also do those things.
b.clue: Focus on who decided he would go, not on what happened after.

a.best: A convict sent from London to New South Wales

b.best: He chose to leave and was not made to go

check.summary: No problems found. The facts on convict transportation and free migration are correct, both questions have one clear answer, and the explanations match the card.
